en: Preface:
This old, tangled vine has been gnawed and chewed by so many people that it is reduced to a hundred fragments; yet it remains perfectly round and whole.
One must not simply draw out the tendrils and pull the vines, nor seek out branches and pluck leaves. I have long applied my mind to this Way. One day—

I have extensively consulted various texts, selecting those that accord with the essential meaning and synthesizing them with my own insights to compile this volume, titled *The Essential Compendium of the Fundamental Teachings*.

My intention is not to foster fragmentation or superficiality, which would leave later generations blind; rather, I desire to provide students with a point of reliance and facilitate their investigation of the truth.
As for the claim that "so-and-so was thus" or "so-and-so was thus," wherein one is five and five is one—this is the core principle.
It is simply this. Its essence and its purport are nothing more than this. I exhort those among my disciples: you should transmit this only in secret.

If it were to be mistakenly passed on to the unworthy, who would then engage in groundless and forced interpretations—whereas the old man of the Three Mountains has already long since committed the error of adding feet to a snake—I dare not do so.
On the full moon of the first month of summer in the year Dingyou of the Shunzhi era, Denglai of Sanshan inscribed this at the Wuyun Abbot’s Quarters.
Written by the elder master Qingzhong Tiebi Ji on the *Five Schools’ Cessation*.
To employ the Linji school while failing to penetrate the Caodong is like being a wild fox;

to employ the Caodong school while failing to penetrate the Linji is to fall into the net of doctrinalism. One must necessarily master both Linji and Caodong, for then Yunmen, Guiyang, and Fayan are contained therein.

*The Essential Compendium of the Five Houses’ Tenets*, Compiled by Chan Master Sānshānlái, Edited by his Dharma Heir from Putuó, Xìngtǒng.
The Linjì School. Volume One.

Chan Master Linji, whose name was Yixuan, was a native of Nanhua in Caozhou. His secular surname was Xing. From childhood he was exceptionally gifted, and as he grew up, he became renowned for his filial piety.
Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he resided at lecture halls, where he thoroughly investigated the Vinaya and extensively studied the sutras and śāstras.
Suddenly, he sighed and said: "This is merely a medical prescription for saving the world; it is not the essential meaning of the separate transmission outside the teachings."
Changing his robes, he traveled to various regions. First, he visited Huangbo; next, he called upon Dayu. The dialogues and exchanges between them are recorded in the *Xinglu* (Record of Conduct).

Having received the seal of approval from Huangbo, he subsequently arrived at a small temple situated by the Hutuo River at the southeastern corner of the city of Zhenzhou in Hebei, where he served as the abbot.
It was because of this location that Linji derived its name. The eighth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty.
On the tenth day of the fourth month in the year of Dinghai, he adjusted his robes, took his seat, and after finishing his dialogue with the Three Sages, passed away in silence.
His disciples constructed a stupa for his entire body in the northwest corner of Daming Prefecture. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huizhao.
The pagoda is named Chengling (Luminous Spirit).

It embodies the Linji tradition: the total functioning of the great capacity, where the staff and the shout are applied simultaneously; like tigers leaping and dragons rushing, it moves with the speed of shooting stars and flashing lightning.

Bearing the spirit of soaring toward the heavens, he employs an extraordinary mode of guidance. Rolling up or unfolding, releasing or seizing, he acts with sovereign mastery over killing and giving life.

He sweeps away emotional views and is utterly liberated from all subtle entanglements. Taking the "True Person of No Rank" as his primary principle, he may employ shouts or blows, or clarify the truth by raising his whisk.

When Linji first arrived at his monastery in Hebei, he met the two senior monks Puhua and Kefu and said to them, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo here; you two may assist me. The two men then respectfully departed.
Three days later, Puhua came up and asked, "What did you say three days ago, Master? Linji struck him.
Three days after that, Ke Fu came up and asked, "Why did you strike Puhua three days ago, Master?
Linji struck him again. That evening, for the small assembly, he said: "Sometimes I take away the person but not the environment; sometimes I take away the environment..."
"I do not seize from others. At times, I seize both person and object; at other times, I seize neither person nor object. He further said:
"When practitioners from various regions come here, I sever their capacities according to three types of root-faculties.
If those of middling or inferior capacity come, I seize their object but do not remove their dharma. If those of superior-middling capacity come, I..."

I may then simultaneously seize both the object and the dharma, as when one of the highest faculties comes before me. Or, I may neither seize the object nor the dharma, as when one with extraordinary insight comes.
Here in this place, I function as the whole body; it does not pass through the various faculties.

O Great Virtue, when you arrive here, even if a student exerts all their strength, there is no way to penetrate it. By the time they have passed through the sparks of flint or the flash of lightning, they have already missed it.
If a student’s eyes flicker or move, they immediately lose the connection. An ancient master further said:

"When those of middling or inferior capacity come, the object is taken away but not the Dharma; when those of middling or superior capacity come, both the object and the Dharma are taken away but not the person;
when those of the highest capacity come, both person and object are taken away; when one who transcends all categories comes, neither person nor object is taken away. Such is the case.
This is called the "Fourfold Discernment. Do you see it? Directly facing one another, the unobstructed realm is presented; in the midst of clashing blades, the person within is fully revealed.
Sanshan said: "Discernment (liao) refers to material. It is like using materials to build a house; there are large and small ones."
The distinction between the crooked and the straight refers to the act of selecting and choosing. It is like the materials for building a house:
one must select which shall serve as the ridgepole and beams, and which shall serve as the rafters and roof-boards; using them according to their respective qualities ensures they are not confused.
The method of receiving people is likewise: one employs them according to their individual capacities. However, among the "Four Selections" (*si liao jian*), there is only the person.

Regarding the two characters for "object" (*jing*), why is the character for "dharma" (*fa*) further added? Generally speaking, "person" (*ren*) refers to that which functions according to its own essence;
"object" (*jing*) refers to that which is pointed out by taking up a thing as it is; and "dharma" (*fa*) refers to that which guides and introduces others according to their capacities.
"To take away" (*duo*) means to exclude and not employ [the term]. One must observe the phrase "at times" (*you shi*).

It is very much alive; it is merely a skillful device for engaging others, applied as the occasion demands, flexible and perfectly integrated, acting in harmony with the Way without deliberate intent.
If one were to examine it closely, there appears to be a distinction between seizing and not seizing.
If one were to insist on grasping a dead snake, deliberating and calculating, one would have already blinded the eyes of people; how could that be the Linji school?
How profound! Students must discern this. Regarding the four kinds of selection in the Jì (Ji) school:
"taking away the person but not taking away the environment"—one's countenance is not permitted to be seen by others; though green and yellow fill the eyes, let the master look as they will.
Sanshanlai said: "Once the Prince has departed, the fragrant grasses turn green. The verse says: "Stealing the person, not stealing the realm:
Cinnabar mixed with rouge. The great earth and the mountains and rivers— Everywhere they manifest their images."
"Seizing the environment, not seizing the person; do not mistake the use of the meditation board and the grass mat. The eyebrows and eyelashes are the truest intimates. San-shan Lai said:
"When the spring in Luoyang has ended, Lü Dongbin arrives. The verse says: "Seizing the environment, not seizing the person."
Holding hands, they travel deep into the night; meeting one another, they do not recognize each other. Face-to-face, there is neither stranger nor kin.
Both person and environment are utterly stripped away. Returning to the abbot’s quarters, he is too weary to open his mouth; descending from the meditation seat, he is too indolent to utter a word.
Sanshanlai said: "The fisherman stays overnight; it is late in the third watch. He offered this verse: "Both man and environment are utterly stripped away;
how can one search for emptiness? The formless golden bullet has struck down all the soaring cranes."
Neither person nor environment can be taken away; raising one's voice in song, it is difficult to fathom. Holding up the staff, it cannot be drawn; San Shanlai says:
"The cowherd boy points afar toward the village of apricot blossoms. The verse says: Neither person nor environment can be taken away.
Free and easy, liberated and untrammeled—his feet tread upon Mount Emei, his tongue speaks of the Five Peaks.
When a monk asked Linji, "What is the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way? Linji replied: "As for the Buddha, it is the purity of the mind.
As for the Dharma, it is the luminosity of the mind. As for the Way, it is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere. These three are one."
All are empty and devoid of reality. Suppose there were a true person on the Way whose mindfulness was uninterrupted from moment to moment.

When the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he was simply seeking someone who would not be deluded by others. Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he was enlightened in a single word;
only then did he realize that his previous efforts had been in vain. As for my own realization today, it is identical to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
There is no difference. If one realizes it through the first phrase, one is capable of being a teacher to Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If one realizes it through the second phrase, one is capable of being a teacher to humans and devas. If one realizes it through the third phrase, one cannot even save oneself.
Sanshan said in his parting words: "If you realize it through the first phrase, you will knock over the lacquer Kunlun at midnight.
If you realize it through the second phrase, you will perform somersaults within the pores of a lotus fiber. If you realize it through the third phrase, a three-year-old child walks with a limp.
These three phrases are all spoken from the standpoint of your own realization; you must examine the first one.
Second, regarding the literal meaning of the second and third words: there are depths and shallows in speech, and there is a gradual progression in discourse.
If one merely muddles it all into a confused mass and makes conjectures out of thin air, one will not understand the words uttered by Linji.
The First Phrase of the Three Phrases of the Ji Lineage: "The seal of the three essentials opens, the vermilion dot is narrow; there is no room for deliberation, for host and guest are distinguished.
Sanshanlai said: "Far! He offered this verse: "The first phrase: closing the door to nod off in sleep; never once did he open his eyes."
At the moment of the eye, one plays in the accomplishment of samādhi. The second line:
How could a wondrous understanding not allow for the question of Wu-cho? How could Upāya fail to respond to the mechanism that cuts through the stream?
San-shan-lai said: "Close. He then offered this verse: The second line: The infant has just begun to draw breath; With a single stroke of strength, he traverses the earth.
The sound comes; the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are complete.
This is the third phrase: "Simply observe the puppet on the stage; its every movement depends entirely on the person inside pulling the strings.
Sanshanlai said, "Wrong. He then offered this verse: Third phrase: Seeking fire, one waits for the fire-drill; it burns away the face.
What benefit is there in such trivialities?

Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "In general, when expounding the Dharma of the Patriarchal School, one must have the Three Mysteries within a single phrase, and the Three Essentials within each Mystery.
There must be the provisional and the real; there must be illumination and function. How do you all understand this?"
Fenyang Shanzhao brought this up and said: "Which one is the phrase of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials?
Sanshanlai replied: "A flying pellet strikes Huanglong; his eyebrows are bitten by a rat."
The Three Mysteries of the Jì School:
The First Mystery within the Mysteries. This is like Zhaozhou’s response regarding the courtyard cypress.
These words do not abide in the essence, nor do they cling to the phrase; their wondrous mystery is inexhaustible. Yet, when the matter does not meet the occasion, it fails to strike home.
It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its shadow sinking into the cold water; thus it is also called "the mystery within function.
Sanxianlai says: "This is like Zhaozhou’s response regarding the courtyard cypress; here, he points directly to what is present before one."
What is brought forth is it; how could it be anything other than plain and obvious? Yet why is it designated as "the most profound within the profound"?

Furthermore, how can one regard the "profound within the profound" as being identical to the "profound within function"? For what reason would there be a principle whereby the "profound within function" constitutes the "first profundity"?

Indeed, in all the chanting and expounding of the *zong* (the fundamental school), there is no word that does not issue forth from the essence (*ti*). There has never been anything that can depart from it.
Regarding the one who expounds the essence of the Dharma: it is simply that the "First Profundity" (Dìyī Xuán) is established as the provisional essence;
this is close to being correct. What, then, is the First Profundity?
Sanshanlai says: "The two shoulders of the Vajra. The verse states: "The First Profundity: the tortoise flies upward."
Heaven! Left with but a single foot, he treads before the time of Wei-yin.
This is the mystery within the second phrase: like Zhang Gong drinking wine while Li Gong gets drunk; three times three before, and three times three after.
Six times six is thirty-six. These words have no conceptual path. Although they arise from within the very substance [of reality], this single phrase is not restricted by that substance.
Sanshanlai said: "The expression 'six times six is thirty-six' is precisely a direct pointing."
How can it be said that there is no intentional path, yet the second phrase is designated as the "Mystery within the Phrase"?
One must know that the "Mystery within the Phrase" of the second phrase is precisely the "Mystery within the Phrase" itself. For there is substance (*tǐ*) before there is function (*yòng*);

whatever is manifested is always the arising of function from substance. Therefore, it is appropriate for function to follow substance; thus, the second mystery is merely provisionally designated as such.
To establish this as the "Mystery within Function" is approximately correct.
What is the second mystery? Sanshanlai said:
"Empty-handed, grasping a golden whip. The verse says: The second mystery—riding a horse up the high mountain.
The Pole. Spraying the ground, he performs a somersault; he hangs down a single coin. The third: The Mysterious within the Body.
This is the very first phrase, which issues forth from the true body. This single phrase already embodies the mystery within the body.
Through words, the principle is revealed, thereby manifesting the essence within the mystery. Although this principle is clarified, [it remains beyond conceptualization].
This is because the capacity (the spiritual faculty) does not depart from its locus.
Sanshan Lai said: "As for the statement that 'the mystery within the essence' is the first phrase, it is manifested from the true essence.
Since it is the first phrase manifested from the true essence, how could one take this phrase of the original true essence [as the ultimate]?"
Is the third mystery the eye? One must know that the third mystery is the mystery within mysteries.
It encompasses both the preceding aspects of essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*), yet it is fully manifested right before one’s face. This is called essence;
it cannot be called function, nor can it be called neither essence nor function. It transcends the realm of thought and language, being difficult to fathom; it is not merely—
Speaking in terms of the essence itself, it would be more accurate to designate the second mystery as the "mystery within mysteries.
What, then, is the third mystery?
Sanshanlai said: "The void plays on a swing. He offered this verse: The third mystery, A whole sphere without center or edge.
The Eastern Sea drifts upon the great ocean, Where a bottomless boat is rigged.
"The foremost requirement: when the wind blows, who dares speak? When the thousand sages arise all at once, how could one exhaust this wondrousness?
San Shanlai said: "Look at this verse; even so, those who attempt to describe the 'profound within the profound' are mistaken."
"What is the first essential?
Sanshanlai replied, "On one's head, one wears a black gauze cap. He then offered this verse: The first essential: Vast and empty, expansive and boundless.
The path is cut off; the mist and waters are cold. How could a traveler ever reach it?
The second essential: A bright mirror stands upon its stand; both Hu and Han find it profoundly useful. A green serpent leaps from its case.
San Shan Lai said: "Look at this verse; it too is intended for the 'Mystery within the Middle,' yet those who speak of it approach it [from the side of the words]."
"What is the second essential?
Sanshanlai replied, "At midnight, the golden rooster crows. He then offered this verse: The second essential: Beauty and ugliness are illuminated all at once;
Transverse and vertical, wondrous functions are distinguished; The Qin mirror shines upon its stand.
The third essential point: "Before the kalpa, there was a single aperture. When one hesitates and asks, "How is it? he claps his hands and laughs aloud.
Sanshanlai says: "Look at this verse; even those who speak of the 'mysterious within the midst of formulating a model' are mistaken."
"What is the third essential?
Sanshan said, "The city streets are bustling. He then offered this verse: The Third Essential: In vain one plucks the vermilion strings;
From flowing water and lofty mountains, He strikes forth the melody of non-arising.
Within the first mystery there are three essentials: a wooden man performs somersaults in the void. Who is it that knows this eight-sided clarity?
Within the first mystery, the first essential: the blue sky splits its brain, the frost is boundless; when a single leaf withers—
Ten thousand leaves wither and fall.
This is the second essential within the first mystery. Heaven and earth are vast and boundless, yet have no fixed location; amidst the chaotic mountains, there is but one mountain high.
The third essential within the first mystery: where the jade dragon is employed, there should be no waves. Ten thousand currents flow, ten thousand currents clear.
The verse says: Heaven is high and earth is deep; their roots are fully exhausted. The layered nets of Indra do not permit discursive argument. At every land, at every moment...
Every dust mote is an inexhaustible treasury; there is no need to snap fingers to knock upon the mysterious gate.
Within the second mystery lie three essentials; do not say the iron ox lacks skill—worry not that it knows nothing of water and grass, nor that it does not know rest.
The first essential within the second mystery: the neighing of an iron horse leaves no trace of its intent. A single wave stirs, and ten thousand waves follow.
The second essential within the second mystery: the lazy wooden ox lies down and forgets water and grass, amidst the piled-up mountains.
The first body is at ease;
the second is the mystery, the third is the essential. The jade hare does not know its own body illuminating the world; atop ten thousand households’ towers, ten thousand households are bright.
The verse says: A wooden man and a stone woman contend over the profound mechanism; even lightning and fire find their laughter slow.
When all things return to their source, they are fully understood; at a single sound, Mount Sumeru is shattered into a hundred fragments.
Within the third mystery there are three essentials: the scenery beyond kalpas, the spring beyond kalpas; unbound by this boundary, they are naturally intimate with one another.
This is the first essential within the third mystery: it cannot be retained on the other side of the void kalpa; it manifests within a single mote of dust.
Bodies as numerous as the atoms of all lands.

This is the second essential within the third mystery: vertically exhausting and horizontally pervading beyond the realm of the Space-King, one wanders alone through the infinite layers of Indra’s net.
The third essential within the third mystery: kicking over empty space without hindrance; amidst the depths of chaotic clouds, the chaotic clouds are at ease.
The verse says: Beyond eons, the numinous branch; beyond eons, the fragrance. A naturally grown herb, inherently cool and refreshing. The two extremes...
"Not being drowned is not what is called marvelous. With one shout, the azure sky penetrates the Great Dharma.
Sanshan said: "If one examines such phrases and verses as these, they divide the Three Mysteries into Nine Essentials.
How could this be the original intent of Linji at that time? Listen to my verse:"
"What are the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials?
Sanshanlai said, "It is bound to cause doubt. He then offered this verse: How can the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials be grasped?
If one attempts to engage them through thought, one misses the mark. Gatye Gatye Saṃgatye, Svāhā Svāhā Svāhā.

Ha! Attached to this mountain hall is the pure discernment of the three mysteries (san-hsüan). Within a single phrase of Linji, the three mystery-gates are complete; within each mystery-gate, the three essentials (san-yao) are contained.
These are the great capacity and great function—how could they be subjected to piecemeal analysis through the definitions of phrases? Thus it is said by those of all quarters.
In the questions and answers on the profound essentials, they are also spoken of directly as the first, second, and third. A verse by Fenyang says:

"The Three Profundities and the Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach. One phrase, luminously clear, encompasses the myriad phenomena."

On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. Since ancient times, the Tower Master has categorized these as the "Mystery within the Body," the "Mystery within the Phrase," and the "Mystery within the Mystery.
Yet, his teaching on the Three Essentials (*sanyao*) failed to take root and was left merely as a matter of deception.
If one were to analyze each point in detail, one would simply be following in the Tower Master’s footsteps; this must be discerned.
Sanshan Lai said: "The essence of Linji’s school lies in the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.
However, because previous masters have categorized them excessively, they have inevitably become quite fragmented. Sanshan Tang’s words are indeed a definitive argument;
it is simply because the term 'Three Mysteries and Three Essentials' appears in Linji’s own words that the Ancient Pagoda Master (Gutaizu) arranged them as such.

The mystery within the essence, the mystery within the phrase, and the mystery within the mystery—these three terms must have their proper place. Yet there is still a logical principle [to be followed]:
for instance, if one takes the first as the mystery within the mystery, the second as the mystery within the phrase, and the third as the mystery within the essence, the sequence is inverted.
Furthermore, it is necessary to divide each mystery into three essentials; this is far too fragmented.
I have already provided individual annotations for each point; can these still be called "Profound and Essential" (*xuanyao*)?

In short, the Profound (*xuan*) is inconceivable, while the Essential (*yao*) refers to the urgent, pivotal mechanism. Within a single phrase, there is both essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*), and their essence and function are difficult to exhaust.
It is thus with the Profound, and it is likewise with the Essential. This is why a single sentence possesses the three profundities.
One mystery encompasses the three essentials; such is the general meaning. Let those who would add legs to a painted snake take heed. One day, Linji asked a monk:
"Sometimes my single shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword; sometimes my single shout is like a crouching lion;
sometimes my single shout is like a probe for a fishing rod or a blade of grass; and sometimes my single shout is not..."
"Use it as a single shout. How do you understand this? When the monk hesitated, Linji shouted.
Sanshanlai said, "If that monk had simply given a shout at that moment, he would have ensured that Linji could not even manage to hesitate."
Regarding the four shouts of the Linji school, there is one shout that is like the Vajra King’s precious sword.
Sanshanlai said: "The 'Vajra Precious Sword' refers to its swift sharpness being difficult to withstand. If it encounters a student..."

With feet entangled and hands bound, the creeping vines of conceptual proliferation stretch on and on; if one does not forget these emotional views, they must be severed at once, head-on, without allowing for any lingering attachment.
Should one involve even the slightest bit of discursive thought, one cannot avoid losing one’s body and life.
"What is the vajra-sword? Sanshan said, "It cuts down demons as soon as it encounters them. The verse says: The vajra-sword admits no room for thought or calculation.
When he brandishes [the staff] directly downward, the void is splattered with blood.
At times, his single shout is like a lion crouching on its haunches.
Sanshan said: "The lion crouching on its haunches does not dwell in caves nor abide in old nests; it is majestic and powerful."
Crouching and squatting, with no reliance whatsoever, he lets out a single roar that splits the heads of the entire pack of beasts. There is no place for you to address him;

there is no place for you to evade him. Should you so much as offend his front, you will fall into his teeth and claws. Like a fragrant elephant charging in full flight, there is no one who can withstand him.
"What is the lion crouching on the ground?
Sanshan said, "Its strength is as heavy as a mountain. The verse says: The lion crouching on the ground; as soon as it is touched, it springs up.
"Protruding claws and fangs—how could they tolerate you?
Sometimes a shout is like a probing rod and shadow-grass.
Sanshanlai said: "A probing rod and shadow-grass means that within a single shout, two functions are possessed. Probing..."
Thus, one examines the student's realization as if probing the depth of water with a pole;
hence it is said, "The probe-rod is in hand. This single shout allows for no investigation and cannot be imitated;
without waiting for another path to be traversed, one has already hidden one's traces and lost one's tracks, deceiving others like a thief. Hence it is said, "The shadow-grass follows the body."
"What is the probing pole and the shadow-grass?
Sanshanlai said, "Gods appear and ghosts vanish. The verse says: "The probing pole and the shadow-grass / Reveal the ugly and reveal the beautiful."
"Brother Zhang, Sister Li. Sometimes a shout is not used as a shout.
Sanshanlai said, "That which is a shout yet is not used as a shout undergoes a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes; it has no fixed beginning."
Nianzi. One may call it the Vajra Sword; one may call it the Crouching Lion; one may call it the Probing Pole and Shadow-Grass.
Like a divine dragon appearing and disappearing, its unfolding and rolling are extraordinary.
Facing it, its head is not seen; following it, its tail is not seen. Buddhas and patriarchs find it difficult to fathom; ghosts and spirits cannot gaze upon it. Although the intent lies therein—
Within a single shout, one actually transcends that shout; this is the most profound and wondrous among the four shouts.
One must examine the two characters "at times" (you shi), for they are extremely lively and do not function in this manner exclusively.
Furthermore, look at the single character "ru" (like/as). It is merely a semblance; it is not that there truly exists such a name or category.
Only when you can turn yourself around within this state will you finally see the working of the old man Linji.
"What is the meaning of 'one shout not functioning as one shout'?
Sanshanlai replied, "It would kill everyone under heaven with doubt. He then offered this verse: "Not functioning as a shout, Tossed about and turned upside down;
If you attempt to ask 'how,' There is absolutely no seam."
One day Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "Students of the Way must be extremely careful. It is like the meeting of host and guest, where there is an exchange of words and discourse.
Sometimes one manifests form in response to objects; sometimes one functions with the whole body; sometimes one employs skillful means through displays of joy or anger;
sometimes one reveals only half the body; sometimes one rides a lion; and sometimes one mounts an elephant king. If a truly authentic student of the Way comes forth..."

He first gave a shout. Then he produced a lacquer basin. The Master of Good Knowledge (the teacher) failed to discern it as an objective condition (*viṣaya*) and instead entered that objective field to put on airs and affectations.
The student shouted again. The former person refused to let go. This is a terminal illness; it cannot be cured.
It is called "the guest looking at the host," or perhaps it is because the Master of Good Knowledge did not produce [the object].
As for objects: whenever a student asks about them, [the teacher] immediately seizes them away. When the student is thus deprived of them, they resist to the point of death and will not let go.
This is the host looking after the guest. Or, there may be a student who encounters a single pure realm;

when this emerges before the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the spiritual friend discerns that it is such a realm, seizes hold of it, and hurls it into a pit. The student says, "Excellent, O spiritual friend! Good.
Zhisheng said: "Alas! You do not recognize good from evil. The student then prostrated. This is called "the host looking at the host.
Or there may be a student who comes before a spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra) wearing a cangue and shackles;

the spiritual teacher further places another layer of cangue and shackles upon him, and the student rejoices. Neither understands the other. This is called "the guest looking at the guest," O Virtuous One.
"What I have raised," said the Mountain Monk, "is all for the purpose of discerning demons and distinguishing the extraordinary, so that one may know the false from the correct.
Sanshan Lai said, "Stop! If guest and host are not established, then what?"
Sanshanlai said: "The mutual regard between guest and host refers to the relationship between teacher and disciple as a pair;
'the guest of guests' and so forth refer to each individual within that teacher-disciple dynamic. One must not fail to understand this."
Regarding the "Fourth Guest among the Four Guests" of the Jì school, Kéfú said: "Leaning on the gate and huddling by the door, they are as if intoxicated;
their speech and breath show no sense of shame. This is the student who lacks nostrils."
"What is the guest within the guest?

This is precisely the compass and square; it is the ultimate goal of the fundamental lineage (*mūla-yukti*). It is the flow of true permanence, outwardly still yet inwardly wavering.

Like tethering a colt or subduing a rat, the former sages took pity on this and established the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) for the sake of the Dharma. Following their delusions, they mistook black for white;
once these inverted perceptions were extinguished, they sincerely resolved to accord with the ancient tracks. Please observe the ancients: when the Buddha-way was about to be perfected, ten...

The kalpa-tree is viewed like the missing tooth of a tiger or the white-footed hind-leg of a horse; because of such inferiority, the precious throne and rare ornaments are treated as objects of prideful distinction.
A wildcat or a white ox—how could they be reached by the skillful power of Houyi, who shoots and hits a target at a hundred paces?

When the points of arrows meet, what has skillful power to do with it? When a wooden man sings and a stone woman dances, this is not reached by consciousness; how could it possibly be contained within it?
Reflect upon this: a minister serves his sovereign, and a son obeys his father. To be disobedient is not filial; to fail to serve is not to be an assistant.

One should act with hidden conduct and employ oneself in secrecy, appearing as if dull-witted or simple-minded. If one can only maintain such continuity, he shall be called the Sovereign among Sovereigns.
Sanshanlai said: "Look at this Jewel Mirror Samādhi; it encompasses the entire Caodong school without exception.
However, I fear that if one follows the current and treats this as a mere oral instruction passed down through generations, it will no longer be the true tenet of the Dongshan tradition.
The ancients transmitted the seal of the mind with such meticulous care; how can those of today brush aside the fundamental tenets with every single maneuver or pivot?"
As for this, who alone could understand it? Upon reading it, one cannot help but heave a great sigh.
Dongshan said to Caoshan, "I personally received the seal of the *Precious Mirror Samādhi* from our late master at Yunyan;
its essential points have been fully exhausted. I now transmit it to you. You must protect and uphold it well, lest it be severed. Only when you encounter a true vessel of the Dharma..."
It may be transmitted, but it must be kept strictly secret; it must not be revealed even in shadow. I fear that if it were to be widely circulated, our school would perish.
In this age of the Dharma’s decline, many people possess only dry wisdom. If one wishes to discern the authenticity of those who have transcended [the mundane], there are three kinds of leakage.
Those present must, at once, possess the true eye.
The Three Seepages and Leaks of the Caodong School (*Seeping water does not stop; leaking objects do not remain full; hence they are called "seepage and leaks"). 1. The Seepage of Views:

When the faculty (*ji*) does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison. This means that if one’s perspective remains stuck in the realm of the knowable (*jñeya*), even if a wondrous awakening occurs, it must be spat out.
If one does not shift one’s station, one will simply sit within a single color (*ekavarṇa*). So it is said: "If you do not turn your station, you will sit in a single color. So it is said.
As for "speaking," it simply means that within one's speech, one has not yet reached perfection; it indicates that one knows others' views are still obstructed.
What is meant by "leakage in one's view"?
Sanshanlai said: "Simply possess a single eye. He also said: "Let it go. The verse says: "The mountains are heavy..."

Layer upon layer of water, water upon water; ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains within a single glance. If you say that waters and mountains are ever-present before the eyes, the traveler’s path remains shrouded in mist.
2. When emotion leaks out and wisdom constantly turns its back, the locus of vision becomes biased and stunted; this is called the incompleteness of the emotional and cognitive spheres.
Stuck in grasping and rejecting, one cannot achieve integration. When discernment and awareness cling to a single extreme, all are merely the surging waves of consciousness in flux.
Regarding matters along the way and at the riverbank: you must, in every phrase, depart from the two extremes and not stagnate in the conditions of emotion.
Only then will there be a path for emergence.
What is meant by "the leakage of emotion"?
Sanshanlai said, "It is like glue and lacquer. He also said, "It would be better to be more lively. The verse says:
"Carrying a wooden board, one has always seen only one side; How much better it is for the eyes to be fully open everywhere. The attachment filling one's breast must be cast out."
As soon as one falls into deliberation, it becomes unfitting.

Third, the leakage of speech: by investigating the subtle, one loses the fundamental source; with the faculty of discernment clouded regarding the beginning and end, one claims that [the truth] is stagnant in language.
Thus, the phrases lose the essential meaning, and one is unable to turn one's body beneath the samādhi of verbal expression. Consequently, the capacity to respond to the occasion remains obscure.
The fundamental principle is not yet perfected. One must penetrate both speech within silence and silence within speech;
only then can the wondrous intent be perfectly subtle and complete. What constitutes a "leakage of speech"?
Sanshan Lai said, "Four upside down, three topsy-turvy. He also asked, "What do you say? The verse says: "When there are words, one must awaken to wordlessness;

To open one's mouth creates a pair, falling into two or three. How much more so when one flounders about, losing the wondrous meaning— Pitiable and laughable is this 'mouth-meditation' (k'ou-t'ou ch'an)."
The Three Paths of the Caodong School for guiding people:
the Bird Path. Where the mouth does not open, the Mysterious Barrier turns; before a word is uttered, the Bird Path is profound.
This is that which does not fall into language—the single phrase prior to sound.
The Mysterious Path: these characters are inscribed in jade seal script, not with a brush; they are carved as golden insignia, not with a blade.
This is the wondrous purport of the Mysterious Sound—discussed yet beyond discussion.
Extending the hand, blinking the eyes, and baring the teeth—the mouth issues its earnest charge. Raising the whisk and striking the mallet, he transmits it with meticulous care.
This is the direct holding up [of the truth] before one’s face; it is brought forth according to the capacity of the occasion.
Sanshanlai said, "It is beautiful indeed, yet there is still one person who utterly refuses to accept it. He then offered this verse:
Moving back and forth through space, its traces are utterly severed; The subtle meaning within the profound is a melody difficult to exhaust.
The eight characters are opened wide without obstruction; Grasp the underlying mechanism, and everywhere there is penetration.
The Three Essential Principles of the Caodong School, Part One:

The Simultaneous Practice of Striking and Singing. "Striking" (qiāo) means to strike; it cuts everything off at once and belongs to the realm of principle (*lǐ*). "Singing" (chàng) means to raise [a phrase];

it is brought forth in tandem with striking and belongs to the realm of phenomena (*shì*). The simultaneous practice of striking and singing means that both phenomena and principle are fully present. This is termed "the biased and the correct" (*piānzhèng*).
"Proceeding together" means that in the Chan school, illumination and function are simultaneous.
What is meant by "proceeding together in both striking and singing"?
Sanshanlai said: "The howling of monkeys and the singing of birds proceed according to their natural spontaneity; before the mountains and behind the ridges, it is all one and the same spring."
The verse says: Striking and singing proceed as one; gathering in and letting go follow the same path. Whether horizontal or vertical, principle or phenomenon, there is no partiality or attachment;
killing and enlivening are clearly distinguished—can you understand this?
2. The Mysterious Path of the Golden Chain. Regarding the "Golden Chain": it refers to a linked succession of rings like hooks and chains, where the bloodlines of continuity are never severed.

Within phenomena (shì), principle (lǐ) is hidden; within principle, phenomena are hidden. Within the partial there is the whole; within the whole there is the partial. Principle and phenomenon are perfectly interfused; the whole and the partial are non-dual.
Interwoven without obstruction, their wondrous responsiveness is inexhaustible; hence it is called the "Mysterious Path."
"What is the mysterious path of the golden lock? Sanshanlai replied:
"Woven into a single piece of natural brocade, so dense that even a golden knife cannot cut it open. He then offered this verse:
"The mysterious gate of the golden lock is reached by few; Its wondrous function is like a ring, applied according to the occasion. Coming and going, it does not..."
Severing partiality and overturning mutual dependence—this single phrase is impartial, transcendent, and marvelous.

3. Not Falling into the Realm of Ordinary or Holy Beings: He sits and cuts off both extremes; phenomena and principle do not intersect. He establishes neither the profound nor the subtle; he does not fall into existence or non-existence.
Responding to things to benefit living beings, he attains great sovereign mastery. All reflected images rely upon him; he strikes them all down at once.
"Deliverance. This clarifies that both [the ordinary and the holy] are gathered together.
How is it that one does not fall into the categories of ordinary or saintly?
Sanshanlai said: "The original face is nothing more than this: eating, drinking, and dressing as one pleases."
The verse says: The noble understanding and ordinary sentiments are crossed out with a single stroke; there is neither affliction nor sorrow.
The face of non-arising remains perfectly whole; why labor so hard to become a horse or an ox?
Caoshan said: "Any perception of the ordinary or the sacred is a golden lock blocking the profound path; one must necessarily employ indirect methods (huìhù).
Now, those who take the food of right livelihood must possess three kinds of 'falling' (duò): first, wearing fur and bearing horns; second, not severing sound and color."
Third, not receiving food. Choubu Na asked: "What kind of falling away is it to have fur and horns? He replied: "It is the falling away of being of that class. He asked:

"What kind of falling away is it to not sever sound and form? He replied: "It is the falling away of following along. He asked: "What kind of falling away is it to not receive food? He replied: "It is the falling away of nobility."
In the Caodong school, there are three kinds of falling.
The first is "falling into the category" (lei-duo), which means wearing fur and bearing horns. "Category" refers to the affairs of the various species;
if one’s mind has any lingering attachments, one cannot avoid falling into the ranks of these different species. One must simply be free of a single thought.
I am about to enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a different species; therefore, my current category must also fall away.
How does this category fall? San-shan Lai said:
"Though one performs the conduct of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal. The verse says: "Wearing fur..."
Wearing horns, he passes through with ease; once he enters the desolate mound, he cannot find him.
Second, not severing sound and form is to fall everywhere. "To follow" means to pursue sound and chase after form—this is not severing sound and form.
If one does not clearly understand sound and form, one cannot avoid falling into the midst of them. One must know that sound does not [arise] of itself...

Sound and form do not constitute themselves as sound and form; sound and form are fundamentally non-existent, provisionally established through the mind. One must not be attached to what is seen or heard;
within sound and form, there must be a path for emergence. Therefore, one must also fall away from them accordingly.
"What is 'falling in accordance'?
Sanshan said, "Seeing form is not a matter of form; hearing sound is not a matter of sound. He then offered this verse:
"Seeing form and hearing sound Are ultimately not the dust of the senses. The oriole sings in the green trees— There is another who understands."
Third, not receiving food is the state of the noble and honorable; receiving food is a matter of this present world. Not receiving food belongs to that other shore.
If one clings to that shore, one has not yet escaped falling into the ranks of the noble and honorable.

One must first fully understand that other shore and then come back to practice on this side. Even the single rank of the noble and honorable must be left empty; therefore, it is called "noble and honorable."
"One must also fall.
"What is the fall of the noble and honorable?
Sanshan said: "Without donning precious or imperial robes, one comes wearing a tattered, ragged shirt. He then recited this verse: "Rituals are transcended,"
The hundred officials were not of high station; there was no one standing in attendance, and he always remained at ease.
Sanshan said, "To 'fall' has two meanings: to fall into existence and to fall away from it. If one remains stagnant within these three [realms], that is falling into existence.
If one can find a way to emerge from within these three, that is falling away. As for the discussion of donning..."
Wearing horns upon one's fur is the "falling into categories. Not severing attachment to sound and form is the "falling into following. Not accepting food is the "falling into nobility.
Such is the meaning of "falling. However, if we discuss Caoshan’s teaching, one must possess the words regarding the three kinds of falling.
Thus, the principle of "falling away" and "removing" is correct, as annotated above. These two meanings encompass both aspects.
Viewing it from approximately three perspectives, one must clarify the stages of transformation before one can attain [realization]. Let those who understand discern this.
If one eats knowing the proper time for eating and does not suffer the harm of improper food, one will not die an untimely death; this is called "right livelihood" (samyag-ājīva). Huangbo said:
"Those who study these days, as soon as they emerge from the assembly, desire only to possess much knowledge and understanding, seeking extensively for literary meanings."
One engages in practice, yet because one does not know that excessive intellectual understanding conversely becomes a poison, it is like giving too much curdled milk to a child;
whether it is digested or not, one knows nothing at all, and thus suffers harm. How could one realize that such intellectual understanding belongs entirely to the realm of arising and ceasing?
Within True Suchness (*tathatā*), this matter fundamentally does not exist. Therefore, Caoshan valued the food of right livelihood and established the "three falls."
Within the three kinds of reed flowers of the Caodong school, there is one kind of reed flower:
its single color reaches the ultimate pure white; neither side is permitted to be touched by blue or yellow.
This is the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where not a single speck of dust is admitted; it is true emptiness beyond all marks.
Even unto this very moment, it is called "the single reed-flower.
There are two kinds of reed-flowers: they do not compete with ordinary flowers, but alone transcend all other grasses in their noble loftiness.

This is not adhering to a single form; it does not abide in the state of correctness. Moving upward with ease, like a crane soaring through the clouds and mists, it escapes the silver cage—this is called "flying out from amidst the reeds."
The three kinds of reeds: green waters and blue mountains are their constant companions; the pure breeze and bright moon are their neighbors by night.
Here, principle and phenomena are blended and fused; they are released as they are gathered. Though existing in the present moment, they do not fall into the present moment.
When the child turns around to join the father, it is called "returning to enter the reeds."
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "A single color reaches the ultimate within the true state; Not abiding in the true state, one exits the silver cage.
Turning the body to join the father, there is no fixed end; In the three kinds of reeds, one does not dwell on effort."
Of the three kinds of reeds outside, the first is the white-horse reed. Turning one’s body, the scenery remains fundamentally unchanged; looking back at the home mountain, it is altogether the same.
This is the utility of clarity.
Second, the bright moon and reeds amidst the frost: their origins in the streams and mountains differ, yet upon returning, the clouds and moon are one and the same;
there is illumination.
Third, snow pressing down upon the reeds amidst the frost: movement and turning are ordinary and level; horizontal and slanting are the fundamental state of suchness.
"Clarity and illumination function as one.
The verse by Sanyanlai says: "There is function and there is illumination; illumination and function are the same. At this moment, the master reveals the point of the needle's tip."
The place where it lightly pricks is inconceivable; it flies into the reeds and its trace is lost.
Regarding the Three Questions and Answers of the Caodong School:
"What is the eye of the skull? The answer says: "The eyes do not blink, yet they illuminate the four quarters with penetrating clarity."
"What is the skull’s ear? He replied, "The ears do not lean; the perfect sound is clearly manifest.
"What are the skull’s hands and feet? He replied, "The arms do not dangle, yet they shatter empty space;
the feet do not move, yet they trample over mountains and seas."
The "skull" refers to a pure body; it signifies the matter pertaining to the side of the Dharma-body. What is the meaning of the answer?
It means that although one does not cling to anything, one is nevertheless able to shatter everything.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "Realizing the Dharma-body, there is nothing to be done; In the state of non-action, function is never deficient.
Transversely manifesting to respond to things, yet truly being nothing at all— Who is it that accords with conditions as they arise?"
The Four Seals of the Caodong School (To distinguish the pure from the turbid, one must discern the harmony of the seals and the wind).
When there is wind but no seal: one greedily gazes at the moon in the sky, yet loses the pearl in one’s own palm.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: Facing the wind, not facing the seal; He breaks through the vast primordial mist, forgetting the state of chaos.
Let his meritorious achievements rise as high as heaven; Who can understand this single melody from the age of Fuxi?
When sealing, do not face the wind; you have grasped the nostrils, yet forgotten the tongue.
San Shanlai’s verse says: When sealing, do not face the wind; One night the Lord of Spring sleeps most soundly.
Red and white fill the garden with no one to tend it; The smiles of the blossoms on the branches are endless.
When both the wind and the seal are properly applied, one shall wear the stars and carry the moon; one shall enter the water and drag through the mud.
A verse from the Three Mountains says: When both the wind and the seal are properly applied, One is neither dazed nor crazed, neither mad nor wild.
The entire body is clad in golden armor, Seeking to engage in a battle with the autumn wind.
"The wind-seal is both inappropriate; Carrying water to sell at the riverhead, Lighting a lamp to assist the sunlight.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "The wind-seal is both inappropriate; Paper screens, stone pillows, and square bamboo beds.
The patched robe covers the head, knowing nothing at all; There is neither short nor long."
Zhang San splits his mouth open to display his spirit; he remembers his eyebrows but forgets his eyes. Deaf and blind, they call out to one another in vain;
the gateway of the face is shattered, cutting off all passage for people.
In the Caodong school, there are four "borrowings.
Borrowing function to clarify status: status is a void status; function is the effort of a single thought over ten thousand years.
To borrow function to clarify status means to borrow the merit of that function to illuminate the fundamental matter.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "The peach and plum trees throughout the garden are in full bloom; Do not say that the Lord of Spring smiles but faintly.
Every form and color emerges, unable to be concealed; In vain, he leaks the mechanism of the Creator."
"Manifesting Function by Borrowing the Position. To manifest function by borrowing the position means to manifest the functioning power by relying upon the original source.
San Shan Lai’s verse says: "From birth, his resolve has been extraordinary; he has performed a feat that reaches the earth and overturns the heavens."
It is not that one harbors great ambitions at all times; how else could one return home wearing brocade?

"Borrowing, borrowing—not borrowing" is the "Coming from the Center. Transcending both vertical and horizontal constraints, one attains the wondrous. Although there is "borrowing, borrowing," in reality there is no borrowing;
essence and function are as one.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: Every dharma, every instance, is naturally heard; There is no distinction between before and after, or center and edge.
Gathering and releasing as they come, unfolding and rolling up as they go— The myriad stars and rivers share a single sky.
Complete transcendence without reliance; not abiding in phenomena, not abiding in principle, not abiding in the profound and subtle, and not abiding in existence or non-existence.
Both essence and function are forgotten; neither the partial nor the absolute is established. This is arriving within the "comprehensive."
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "Upon reaching the point of 'only this,' there is simply 'only this. Not a single thing remains that can be sought.
Within this, how could one discuss the profound and subtle? Only when principle and phenomena are no longer related does one reach the ultimate end."

In the Caodong school, there are four [levels of] "knowing there is": knowing there is while not yet knowing there is; the vast expanse of karmic consciousness where there is no fundamental basis to rely upon;
knowing there is; and when a single thought reflects back its light, one immediately returns to what was originally attained.
Knowing existence, one does not know existence; when one reaches the state of no-mind, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Only after not knowing existence does one truly know existence; then one will believe Nanquan’s calling it a "cow."
Sanshanlai’s verse says: Many obscure the matter of their original nature; If one day they see it, they will avoid wasting time.
Do not say you are leisurely and carefree once you have returned home; What can be done about wearing horns and being covered in fur?
In the Caodong school, there are two turns and one pivot:
The first turn: Casting aside the idle scenery on this side, one turns back to behold the fine vista beyond.
The second turn: All day long the door remains closed, weary of waiting for guests; suddenly the door is opened to question the traveler.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: Wandering through rivers and lakes for several decades, I have returned to lie high upon the white clouds.
One morning, suddenly stirred by thoughts of the dusty world, I once again board my raft to drift with the waves.
In the Caodong school, there is "borrowing phrases and carrying along.
As for "borrowing," it means to rely upon that which is external in order to manifest one's functional efficacy. This is the position of partiality; this is the external succession.
This is the lineage of the ministers.
As for the phrase "sentence by sentence": the first sentence within clarifies its fundamental essence. This is the position of rectitude; this is the internal succession;
this is the royal lineage.

"Carrying along": "Carrying along" means holding and borrowing phrases. Two kinds are borrowed and practiced together, proceeding from the partial position and ultimately returning to the correct position.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: It is not that one does not see spring because there are no flowers; when spring arrives, the flowers are as fresh as ever.
Who is the master over the blooming and falling of the flowers? Once this is clearly understood, one may act with total freedom.
In the Caodong school, the five minor ranks are attained when great function (*da-gōng*) is first turned. "Function" (*gōng*) refers to efficacious application.

When deluded thoughts arise during the twelve periods of the day for a practitioner, they should illuminate and realize them with the awakened mind, just as a general is rewarded for his achievements by the three armies. If deluded thoughts are extinguished...
Eliminate it; even true illumination is non-existent. It is like a general who has achieved merit and is rewarded by the Emperor.

If both the real and the false are forgotten, and neither the orthodox nor the deviant is established, one does not cling to nobility. This is like an Emperor who, having achieved great merit, cannot be rewarded by anyone else.
Therefore it is said: "Great merit is not rewarded. Great merit is the merit of non-merit; this is a provisional position.
As soon as one turns, one enters from within the provisional position. Thus, one is born by borrowing the position.
Born through the borrowed position, having already completed the great function, one then returns to enter the birth-state.
Although being born as the legitimate son is inherently the lineage of a king, yet in relation to the sovereign, one must be called a subject and thus belongs to the lineage of subjects.

This also belongs to the category of "borrowed positions. This means that even if another person resides in the Eastern Palace (the heir apparent), they still occupy a partial position and cannot occupy the primary position;
having attained great merit, they have instead entered a partial position.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: As soon as one speaks of "no-effort," one has already entered the realm of effort; When effort and no-effort are exhausted, the wondrous is difficult to fathom.
A single step turning back is not a matter of another; One gradually enters the deep palace, drawing near to the ninefold gates.
If the "single color" (*ekavarṇa*) is extinguished, one is born as the Empress of the Central Palace. The Crown Prince must reside in the Eastern Palace.
The Eastern Palace refers to the affairs at the edge of the single color; it is the movement from the partial toward the central.

If one dwells in this intermediate space, one is neither called noble nor established in the correct position. Therefore, the single color must be completely extinguished so that one does not dwell in the Eastern Palace. Not...
Only by guarding one’s nobility can one be called noble;
only then is one truly called noble. It is like a crown prince who only attains the title of noble after the Emperor has passed away and he succeeds to the throne.

Likewise, if a practitioner of the Way, though clear regarding their fundamental nature, cannot integrate it with every situation but remains fixedly seated within a conceptual nest, they are not yet truly noble.
The interior is called "having ground. Where there are positions and tracks, one must not dwell;

rather, one must turn around and travel another path, without lingering in the profound and subtle, and without clinging to the center or the periphery. Though situated in a position of honor and nobility, one does not abide therein.
Only then can one be called noble and honored; otherwise, countless people would be drowned in the stagnant waters of death.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "The original nature is Buddha—there is no need for doubt; yet to recognize it as such remains the delusion of ignorance."
Having trampled through the crown of the head until there is nowhere left to seek, it stands forth grandly revealed, presiding over the imperial capital.
To "shift one's feet within the subtle" means to reach the true principle; yet even this must be cast aside.
One must not harbor thoughts of it being extraordinary, nor thoughts of it being mysterious and wondrous. What preceded this was but a single color.

Once this has been eliminated, these phenomena are exhausted; now, even true reality (*tattva*) is removed. This directly causes both principle and phenomena to be forgotten together, so that neither truth nor delusion is established.
Therefore, it is called "shifting the feet within the subtle."
A crane emerges from its silver cage; being able to shift its feet within the fine [mesh], it naturally does not abide in phenomena, nor does it abide in principle.
Not abiding on this shore or that shore, where is there room for mysterious subtlety? What need is there to look back at the Buddhas and Patriarchs? It overturns the great ocean.
Kicking over Mount Sumeru: a thousand hands cannot lift it; a thousand eyes cannot see it.
If you can realize it here, it is like a crane emerging from a silver cage.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: When both principle and phenomena are forgotten, it is wondrous and extraordinary; To take a single step beyond the self is even more inconceivable.
A crane escapes its silver cage and soars into the clouds and mists; This is precisely the moment of unimpeded flight through the void.
Turning within the station, one transcends emotion and leaves behind views; not involving existence or non-existence, this is the matter of the true station (*samyaktva-pada*).

Although one remains in the true station, one must nevertheless turn back and come from within the partial station (*viparyāsa-pada*). If one were to perpetually block the vital ford, it would not yet constitute the fundamental division [of the Way];
therefore, one must extend a hand at the head of the path of the present age to receive others. Only thus can one benefit oneself and benefit others.
It may be so. "The moon spreads across the golden ground" means that there is both illumination and function. Entering the mud and entering the water, he disregards his own life and body;
appearing through transformation in response to capacities, he gathers in sentient beings. Having finished his work on the other shore, he returns to this shore to receive them.

Benefiting sentient beings through material things; acting with deliberate artifice for the sake of the present age; employing provisional skillful means—this is the wondrous function of turning the body.
San Shan Lai’s verse says: "How often have you not sat by the crags to extinguish the mind's ashes? Yet once again, you must run back through the red dust."
It was not white clouds that startled the dream to an end; for what reason is the moonlight filling the high terrace?
Regarding the first of the Three Phrases of the Mysterious Sun:
the phrase of ordinary non-arising—white clouds cover the green mountains; the green mountains do not reveal their peaks.
One must know that this phrase requires a single path to be penetrated. Once it is penetrated, it is like a lion’s roar.
As San Shanlai’s verse says: "The meaning of the ordinary phrase is profound and mysterious; when the words of non-arising are uttered, there is a separate heaven."
The words fall below and precede speech; they are difficult to grasp. A path that bypasses to the side lies before the pivot of the occasion.
2. The Wondrous and Mysterious Line Without Partiality: The jeweled palace is empty, with no one standing in attendance. By not planting the *wú-tóng* tree, one avoids the arrival of the phoenix.
One must know that this line has neither guest nor host. To penetrate it is like a lion’s backward leap.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: Tracing no tracks and concealing one’s form, one is utterly like a fool; Neither host nor guest is established—this is most profound and subtle.
Deeply secluded, the ancient hall is locked by azure mists; This single phrase, free from self-interest, is the supreme device.
3. The Sentence of the Essential Body’s Luminous Exhaustlessness: When the finger points to space, heaven and earth turn. The stone horse emerges from the gauze cage upon the return journey;
one must know that this sentence carries both meanings together. To penetrate it is like a lion crouching on the ground.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "Flowers bloom upon the withered tree, fresh as brocade; The orders of the three springs arrive, and the warbling birds cease.
If one can casually penetrate its essential meaning, Its essence and function are luminously inseparable."
Dongshan’s initial four statements begin with:
"One: not unfolding the matter. This refers, for example, to his reply to the question about where he was from, when he said, "I am from Zhenzhou; I have brought out a large radish.
These words never unfold or elaborate upon the matter itself; one must understand it beyond the realm of words.
2. Words that do not meet the occasion: This refers, for example, to answering "a dry dung pellet. Such words do not accord with the capacity of the interlocutor;
one must attain wondrous awakening within the space between the words and phrases.
3. Those who rely on words lose [the truth]. If one takes up the matter based on verbal phrases, one immediately loses the fundamental meaning.
This refers to those who are unable to comprehend it beyond the words.
4. Those who stagnate in phrases are deluded. This refers to being stuck within the words, whereby one becomes muddled regarding the true principle.
One who cannot achieve wondrous awakening within the discourse will, despite attaining some realization through these four types [of approaches], remain a merely liberated monk;
if one does not understand this, one will ultimately end up as a mere blunderer.

To rely on words and linger in phrases is ultimately useless; With the mind concentrated as a single piece—what can be done?

Fushan Yuanluo Gong’s Sixteen Topics:
One, Recognizing One’s Own Lineage. To recognize one’s own lineage means one must recognize the fundamental intent of the source, which does not fall within the reach of verbal explanations.
As soon as one attempts to deliberate or measure it, there are thousands of mountains and ten thousand rivers.
2. Reviving from Death. As for "reviving from death": cold ashes flare up with flame; a withered tree wafts fragrance.
One must indeed revive within death. A wooden man claps his hands; a stone woman laughs aloud.
3. Dying Amidst Life. Those who die amidst life are those who, in their greed, pursue the paths of words and thereby lose the person of original nature.
This refers to the "boundary-words" (jing-yu) of Jia Shan; one must directly take them as the discourse on the boundary itself.
IV. Not Falling into Life or Death. "Not falling into life or death" means not sitting at either extreme and not abiding in any single form.
In the ordinary course of daily life, one is carefree and autonomous.

V. The Five Liberations (Pañca-vimokṣa). Regarding the five liberations: one turns the back on phenomena and abandons principles, sweeping away both the holy and the ordinary so that not even a speck of dust remains.
Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations, it is starkly clear and nakedly pure; majestic and unhindered, it reaches its ultimate fulfillment throughout the entire body.

Six. Non-Relinquishment. As for non-relinquishment: it means to wear fur and bear horns, to pull plows and drag harrows, and to sport at will according to the times, without abandoning the principles of phenomena.
This is what is called "recognizing the nature while following the current"; there is neither joy nor sorrow.
7. The Living Man’s Sword. As for the Living Man’s Sword: in all speech, one does not meet with its sharp edge;
one turns wondrously according to circumstances and responds to things with perfect completion. What is called "letting go" means that even tiles and pebbles give off light.
If you can turn yourself around, then naturally you will raise your eyebrows and breathe freely.
8. The Sword that Kills People. As for the sword that kills people: it sweeps away the views of Buddhas and patriarchs and severs the sentiments of sages and ordinary folk.
A single phrase cuts off the current; ten thousand functions are brought to rest. It is said: "If you grasp it firmly, heaven and earth lose their luster.
If you touch its sharp edge, you cannot avoid losing your body and life.
9. Ordinary (Píngcháng). As for the ordinary: it is to act with hands hanging down amidst the routines of daily life, without pursuing anything extraordinary, lofty, or remote.
It is as the saying goes: "When the autumn wind arrives as usual, people feel cool without intending to; they are cool of themselves."
10. Benefiting the Path and Rescuing Beings. "Benefiting the Path and Rescuing Beings" means to cut away the threads beneath one's feet and point out the pearl within the palm.
To rescue all living beings, one benefits them with the Great Way. Although the spring colors have no high or low, in the end, the flower branches are short or long.
11. No Fault in Speech. Regarding "no fault in speech": whether speaking coarsely or subtly, whether employing inversions or playful turns of phrase, one always hits the mark.
This is what is meant by the saying, "Though one's words fill the world, there is no fault in the mouth.
One must only fear that those who cling to words and become stuck on phrases will miss the point right here.
12. Penetrating Liberation. As for "penetrating liberation," it means not being bound by anything whatsoever, but transcending all in a sudden leap.
Having severed the red thread at one's heels, one flies with sovereign ease through heaven and among men. This is what a student of the Way must be able to comprehend.
13. Penetrating Liberation and Non-Penetrating Liberation. Regarding penetrating liberation and non-penetrating liberation:
although one has shattered a jade ball, one still scatters gold dust into one’s eyes; this is non-penetrating liberation within penetrating liberation.
14. Praising. As for "praising," it means to uphold this matter and skillfully proclaim its fundamental principles.
One must be such a person who can understand and awaken beyond sounds. As it is said: "The myriad pipes have hearts, yet they cannot hear;
the solitary crag has no ears, yet it knows the sound."
15. The Section on Subduing Speech. Regarding "subduing speech": it means severing the flow of words and refraining from unrestrained talk.
This is what is meant by closing the mouth and firmly restraining the tongue, settling the body in the foremost position.

16. Entering the Square into the Circle. Regarding "entering the square into the circle": vertically and horizontally one attains the sublime; left and right one encounters the source. There is no further obstruction;
whatever emerges from the mouth is acceptable. One is thus able to enter the Samādhi of Perfect Penetration.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: Having exhausted all frugality and endured bitter toil, who is this person who shares in life and death?
Who knows the depths of this single heart of compassion? Time and again, facing the critical moment, they act with total freedom.

The Guiyang School:
Chan Master Guishan Lingyou. His secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Changxi. He received the Dharma from Master Baizhang Huaihai.
When he first arrived at Mount Daogui, he lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams; it was only after more than ten years that he met Chan Master Yangshan Huiji.
Together they revitalized the Way; thus, all quarters refer to it as the Guiyang School.

The style of the Guiyang School is that father and son form a single family, with teacher and disciple singing and responding to one another. Speech and silence are not revealed; light and darkness race against each other.
Body and function are both manifested; the "Tongueless Man" is taken as the primary principle, clarified through the Perfect Circle (Yuanxiang).
The origin of the Perfect Circle and its manifestation began with National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang, who transmitted it to his attendant Danyuan. Danyuan received the prophetic mandate.
Recorded. This was transmitted to Yangshan, who subsequently established what became known as the Weiyang School. It has six general names:
*yuanxiang* (round symbols), *anjī* (dark triggers), *yihai* (ocean of meaning), *zihai* (ocean of characters), *yuyu* (intentional speech), and *milun* (silent discourse). Danyuan said to Yangshan:
"The National Teacher transmitted ninety-six *yuanxiang* from the Sixth Patriarch to me. The National Teacher then passed away.
At that time, he spoke to me again, saying: "Thirty years after my passing, a śrāmaṇera shall come from the south and greatly propagate this Way.
Transmit it in succession so that it does not become extinct. I have examined this prophecy; the matter rests with you personally.
I now entrust it to you; you must uphold it. Having received it, Yangshan subsequently burned it. One day, he spoke to Yangshan once more, saying:
Yuan said, "The circular diagrams you have just transmitted should be kept strictly secret. Yang said, "I have already burned them.
Yuan said, "These are the diagrams transmitted by the Buddhas down to the present day; why have you burned them? Yang said, "I looked at them once and already understood their meaning.
One must be able to use them before one can obtain them; one must not cling to the original text. Yuan said, "For you, it may be so, but what about those who come after? Yang said:
"If the Master wishes, I shall record it again. He then recorded it once more and presented it to Danyuan, ensuring there was not a single error.
Sanshanlai’s verse says: "The National Teacher and his son were truly causeless; the prophetic records have been transmitted down to this very day."
He painted ninety-six circles; they were like the blue sky and white sun changing people's eyes.
Yangshan had personally received these ninety-six kinds of circular signs from Danyuan. Later, at the place of Guishan...
This mark represents sudden enlightenment. There is a saying that goes: "The secret seal of all Buddhas—how could it be contained within words? It is also said:

"I attained the essence at Danyuan’s place and attained the function at Guishan’s place; this is called 'father and son meeting in resonance. Therefore, there are circular marks used to discern the person.
To draw the character for 'ox' [牛] within the circle is to follow one's own intent; to draw the character for 'Buddha' [佛] within the circle is to seize the other's intent."
Sometimes he draws a person inside a circle; this signifies a refusal to grant full consent. Sometimes he draws a *svastika* inside a circle; this signifies granting full consent.

Sometimes he draws this symbol, sometimes he dots it through, sometimes he slashes it, sometimes he throws it away, or sometimes he wipes it out—all of these are ways of cutting off the flow of conceptual streams.
Furthermore, there are various other signs, none of which fail to represent the host and guest, the methods of yielding and seizing, or the mechanisms of the provisional and the real. In total:
Observing the timing and conditions, one seizes upon and employs them according to the capacity of the individual; this is entering the marketplace with hands extended, establishing skillful means.
Furthermore, when at leisure, teacher and disciple engage in debate, exchanging sharp flashes of wit. It is valued solely that the Great Function manifests before one, free from fixed rules.
One day, a monk from India came to visit. Yangshan drew this symbol (a circle) on the ground and showed it to him.
The monk stepped forward, added another mark (making it a zero), and then wiped it away with his foot. Yangshan then extended both hands. The monk shook out his sleeves and departed.

Sanshan said, "Such a tangled web—what kind of idle furniture for playing with monkeys is this?
Nevertheless, everyone must understand it thoroughly."

It is not separate from the *gūḍhakāya-samādhi* (the samādhi of concealing the body). All such instances are of the same category as the "ocean of meaning.
