It corresponds [to the previous]. This manifests the appearance of the full moon. This sign is called the "Sign of Embracing the Jade to Seek its Appraisal.
If this sign is brought forward as a question, one should answer by writing the character *si* (private) therein. This sign is called "Seeking a Good Mirror.
When the respondent recognizes the jade, they immediately take action. [○@ㄙ] This is named the "Sign of the Hook Entering and the Rope Continuing. If this sign is brought forward...
Question: Simply add the character *ren* (亻) to the side of the character *si* (厶) to answer. This is the questioner’s hooking-in and the respondent’s drawing-out;
it is called the "Phase of Completing the Precious Vessel. [○@(俬-禾)] This is called the "Phase of the Already Completed Precious Vessel.

If one brings this phase forward as a question, simply write the character *tu* (土) within it to answer. [○@土] This is called the "Phase of the Mysterious Seal and Mysterious Principle," which is uniquely liberated.

It transcends all phenomenal characteristics and is not encompassed by the intent of the teachings. If one is of keen and sharp capacity, it is handed over face-to-face; yet if one attempts to grasp it through conceptualization, it is not seen.
The Third Patriarch said: "A difference of a hair’s breadth leaves heaven and earth as far apart. If one does not possess the eye [of wisdom], [one will fail].
How can one distinguish this?

Sanshan Lai said: "There is indeed no lack of 'the profound question' and 'the profound answer,' but if one remains stuck solely within them, one cannot avoid becoming like a mold that has been cast and stripped away.
How could this be considered the ultimate principle of our school? Thus spoke the student.
It is appropriate to grasp the Master’s intent and put it into practice.
A verse by Sānshān Lái says: "One person picks up, one person completes; two by two they accompany each other, each on their own side."
When one recognizes the point where the two sides coincide, it is gathered back as before, the full orb of the moon.
To discern the eighth consciousness:
these are the six consciousnesses possessed by sentient beings; adding the consciousness of space makes the seventh consciousness. As for the seventh consciousness...

It may be designated as the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). It is also called the eight princes (*aṣṭa-rājakumāra*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), and the eight great men (*aṣṭa-puruṣa*).
In total, it possesses the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa*)—four sets of eight. These are the marks of fruition (*phala-lakṣaṇa*), being the merit of the retribution of causal wisdom.

The seventh consciousness is also called the "transmitting consciousness" (*saṃprāpaka-vijñāna*), for the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are inseparable; the former acts as the vanguard when coming, and the latter serves as the rear guard when departing.

Thus, one traces back to the past, clings to the present, and dwells upon the future; the three subtleties and six coarsenesses, the five mental consciousnesses and the six defilements, and the seven consciousnesses—all these are distinguished as "that" and "this," or as "right" and "wrong.
The eighth, the *ālaya-vijñāna*, is called the "pure white consciousness" (*vimala-vijñāna*).
It is fundamentally without flaw or blemish; there is no Buddha and no sentient beings, no "you" and no "I. As an ancient master’s verse says:
The *ālaya* is pure and originally free from delusion; when the three subtle divisions unfold, the six coarse aspects arise.

From this, the eighty-four thousand [afflictions] emerge, and one becomes an ordinary person within the great trichiliocosm as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The fetters of the dreaming mind were never there to begin with; how could the empty flowers seen by diseased eyes truly exist?
In the space of turning over one's hand, the ten wholesome deeds are accomplished—just as one recovers the dark pearl from the red water. Thus it is with the eighth consciousness as well.

It is named the *ālayavijñāna*. For one who has realized the fundamental ground, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform within the state of cause, while the fifth and eighth consciousnesses are perfected upon the fruition.

The sixth consciousness transforms into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), and by reflecting back upon the eighth consciousness, it becomes the Wisdom of Immovability (*āniñjyajñāna*). It is empty, with neither interior nor exterior.
It is named the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is identical in essence [to the other wisdoms]. The Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is the general designation.

Through the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), the six sense organs, the six sense objects, the six consciousnesses, and even the eighty-four thousand afflictions are subsumed; these are then transformed into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The All-Accomplishing Wisdom is further transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality.
The Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) transforms into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); these are of one essence.

Regarding this, if a master of the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇavāda*) is able to effect such a transformation when questioned or challenged, in which consciousness does that transformation occur? According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha instructed Mahāmati:

"During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, you should always purify the manifesting stream of consciousness with the Wondrous Observing Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and transform the six [consciousnesses]."

The sense-faculties (*indriya*) constitute the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Just as when a hand is turned upward, one should not ask where the downward-turned hand has gone;
and just as when water becomes ice, there is no difference in substance, it is said that "afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*).

Regarding the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, take only their meaning and do not cling to the words. The Sixth Patriarch’s verse says: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure."
Purity. The Mind of Equality is free from affliction; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees that there is no effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing Action is identical to the Great Perfect Mirror.
Regarding the transformation of the fruits and causes of the five, eight, six, and seven [consciousnesses]: it is merely a transformation of names, devoid of substantial nature.

If one leaves no lingering attachment at the point of transformation, then amidst all bustling activity, one eternally abides in the *nāga-samādhi*. (6) The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; (7) the Wisdom of Equality.

Wisdom transforms according to its basis. The five [wisdoms] transform upon the fruition of the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), while the eight [wisdoms] transform upon the fruition of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Regarding the "Three Kinds of Kindling the Lamp" (this is found in the Records of Caoshan; it is not the words of Yangshan. Because it was previously included in the Weiyang School, I do not wish to move it).
Caoshan said: "Before the kindling of the lamp, there is a certain state. First, being unaware of its existence, it is like milk mixed with blood."

The first is the knowledge of existence (*asti-jñāna*). It is like obtaining the original object for the very first time when the mind has not yet been stirred; this is called "before the lighting of the lamp.
There is another kind of knowledge of existence that pertains to coming and going, speech, sounds, forms, right and wrong; it does not belong to correct illumination, nor can it be recorded as such.
It is like milk from blood of the same species; this belongs to the side of leakage (*āsrava*) and loss. This is called "after the lighting of the lamp. It is simply...
When the affairs of the three periods of time are exhausted and internal and external attachments are forgotten, one attains an uninterrupted state;
this is the beginning of attaining the true illumination of the lamp, which is called "receiving the prediction" (as recorded in the *Zuting shiyuan*).
"What is it like before the lamp was lit? Shoushan said: "All Buddhas are behind me. Zhimen Zu said:
"In the empty kalpa, there is no idle person. Wuzu Yan said: "It leaves people with lingering doubt."
"What is it like after the lamp has been lit? Shan said, "All Buddhas are behind me.
Zuo said, "The patch-robed monk runs all over the world. Yan said, "A scene of utter embarrassment."
"What is it like to truly light the lamp? The Mountain Master said: "In the green mountains, there is no divergent path. Fuzhao said: "A spark enters the Ox and Dipper constellations.

Verse: Understanding attained, the bright pearl rolls upon the platter; Yet how many difficulties remain unpierced!
Like pouring water from one vessel into another without a drop left behind, One gazes with cold indifference at the scenery across the sea (before the Lamp-Lighting).
Verse: The bright pearl is not seen as it runs upon the platter; The vast sky and still night are dark and boundless.
Through ten ages, past and present, there is neither increase nor decrease; Lifting up the ox’s head, place it upon its tail (after Rán-dēng).
Verse: The questions are clear, the answers are intimate; In every dust mote, in every land, you meet him everywhere.
A single cry of a yellow bird beyond the green mountains— He monopolizes the splendor of spring and becomes its master. (Zhengrandeng)
Sanshanlai said: "Setting aside for a moment what precedes and follows, you must directly cause both illumination and forgetting to vanish;
even so, there is still a slight margin of difference. He spoke in verse: The lamp before and after do not depend on one another; This very lamp is slightly more intimate than the former.
When sentiments across the three periods of time are forgotten and there is no dwelling, One majestically beholds the person of original nature.
The Verse on the Three Illuminations of Incense-Severe (Xiangyan):
Illumination is the original state; To conceive a thought or open one’s mouth is to be separated by mountains and rivers. Even silence and speechlessness are rebuked.
Unfolding it is infinite and inexhaustible; Rolling it back leaves no trace, yet already there is much.
Tranquil illumination, unmoving like a mountain, all affairs come to rest. The clear pool reaches its depths, never flowing away. Within this state, right mindfulness continues perpetually;
the moon is bright in the heart of heaven as clouds and mist are withdrawn.
Constantly illuminating, it is never deficient within the four modes of deportment; from ancient times to the present, there has never been a moment of interruption.

These refer to the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. The Dharma-body is Vairocana; this is translated as "Pervading All Places."

Within the bodies of sentient beings, these are precisely stillness, illumination, and function. Stillness is the Dharma Body (Dharmakāya); illumination is the Reward Body; and function is the Transformation Body.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states that all Tathāgatas possess three bodies, which fully encompass [all manifestations].

Regarding the reception of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): when the Tathāgata was formerly on the stages of practice, he cultivated various dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings and attained the power of mastery.

This is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). As for the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), it refers to the Tathāgatas teaching the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to all bodhisattvas, causing them to understand that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are of one flavor.
It is for the purpose of removing the fear of sentient beings who hold to the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and for inspiring joy in them;
